# Experiment setup {#sec-experiment_wp2}

We adopt a two-stage experimental design. The numerical experiment evaluates TCKF against known latent demand, while the empirical experiment uses monthly LMIS data from Côte d’Ivoire to assess performance under real-world operational constraints. An overview of the experimental framework is provided in **E-companion, Section 4**.

## Forecasting Methods

We benchmark our TCKF model against a suite of standard statistical (Naïve, Mean, Exponential Smoothing State Space (ETS), ARIMA, Syntetos–Boylan Approximation (SBA), and Linear Regression (LR)), machine learning (LightGBM), and foundational (TimeGPT) models. In the empirical experiment, we also include operational baselines: the official LMIS System-Generated Forecast and the human Demand Planner-Adjusted forecast. Full descriptions of these benchmarks, their implementations, and parameter settings are detailed in **E-companion, Section 2**. These benchmarks were selected based on prior evidence in contraceptive forecasting [@hewage2025].

Our forecasting target is monthly latent demand for each product at each facility. We assume no censoring during the forecast horizon because future stockouts and service interruptions are unknown at the time of forecasting. For most models, we evaluate versions with and without regressors that identify the historical censoring regime. The candidate models are summarised in **E-companion, Section 2**.

## Forecasting and inventory setup

The Côte d’Ivoire family planning supply chain includes healthcare sites, district-level warehouses, national warehouses, national supply planners, and donor/programme partners. Healthcare sites record stock movements, consumption, stockouts, and refill needs, and submit monthly reports and requests. District and national planners review and coordinate these requests, while national warehouses distribute stock to district warehouses and facilities. Donor and programme partners support upstream procurement and commodity availability. The system is therefore primarily pull-based because the initial replenishment signal comes from facilities, but it also includes planner review and adjustment before stock is distributed. A high-level supply chain map is provided in **E-companion, Section 3**.

In line with current practice in Côte d’Ivoire, where healthcare facilities determine refill quantities and submit monthly forecasts and order requests one month in advance, we set the forecast horizon to $h = 1$. This enables a direct comparison with both System-Generated and Demand Planner-Adjusted forecasts. In our forecasting setup, we use a time series cross-validation approach with a rolling-origin and an expanding training window. For the **numerical experiment**, each time series uses the first 70 observations for training, and the next 30 observations for evaluation. For the **empirical experiment**, the training period spans from January 2016 to December 2018, and the test period covers the entirety of 2019. At each iteration, the model is trained on all data up to time $t$, and used to forecast the next period. This setup provides a robust view of forecast accuracy across varying demand conditions [@svetunkov2023].

To ensure consistency across models, we generate prediction intervals using conformal prediction. This matches the structure of the proposed TCKF model, which also uses a conformal prediction layer for uncertainty estimation. For LMIS forecasts and planner adjustments, which are provided as point estimates, we apply conformal prediction as post hoc to produce comparable uncertainty intervals.

For the inventory simulation, we model a monthly periodic-review lost-sales system with a fixed lead time of one month ($L=1$), consistent with the replenishment cycle in Côte d’Ivoire. At the end of each month $t$, after demand is realised, a facility places an order $q_t$ that becomes available in month $t+1$. Replenishment decisions are based on the inventory position $IP_t$ (on-hand plus pipeline stock) [@bijvank2011]. With $L=1$, pipeline stock equals the order placed in the previous month, and hence $IP_t = I_t + q_{t-1}$. Under an order-up-to policy with target level $U_t$, orders follow $q_t=\max{0, U_t - IP_t}$, and any demand exceeding available inventory is treated as lost sales.

We evaluate a structured set of benchmark replenishment policies that vary only in how the target level $U_t$ is determined. These include: (i) an as-is policy reflecting current LMIS practice (three-month buffer based on a point forecast) [@hewage2025]; (ii) an uncertainty-aware base-stock policy that sets $U_t$ using forecast quantiles derived via conformal prediction [@babai2025]; (iii) lost-sales heuristics commonly used in practice (myopic variants) [@bijvank2011]; and (iv) an oracle benchmark that uses the latent demand process to provide an upper bound on achievable inventory performance under the same operating constraints [@sachs2014]. We do not attempt to solve for a globally optimal dynamic inventory policy; rather, these benchmarks are used to assess how forecast quality and uncertainty quantification translate into replenishment performance in a standardised lost-sales setting. Full descriptions of the inventory policies are provided in **E-companion, Section 4**.

Alongside the model-based forecasts, we also include the System-Generated and Demand Planner-Adjusted forecasts in the inventory simulation to enable a full comparative analysis in empirical evaluation. We do not use actual stock movement records for inventory simulation, given the influence of external factors such as delivery delays and upstream stock availability at district warehouses. 

The base case simulation assumes a one-month lead time because the Côte d’Ivoire LMIS follows a monthly review cycle, where facilities submit forecasts and order requests one month in advance. Therefore, $L=1$ represents the planned replenishment cycle. However, in practice, replenishment can take longer because of delivery delays, incomplete fulfilment, or upstream stock availability constraints.

To check the one-month lead-time assumption, we used the stock movement data to construct an approximate lead-time proxy. We compare the base case with fixed lead times of two and three months and a stochastic scenario based on the observed receipt delays. Full details are provided in **E-companion, Section 4**.

## Performance evaluation

We assess point forecast accuracy using Forecast Value Added (FVA) based on relative RMSE, and probabilistic forecast accuracy using pinball-loss Skill Scores. Both measures are expressed relative to TCKF, with positive values indicating better performance. In the numerical experiment, true demand is known, allowing evaluation in both censored and uncensored periods. The empirical forecast and inventory comparisons use uncensored observations, where recorded stock distributed is treated as observed demand.

For the inventory evaluation, we focus on the trade-off between product availability, unmet demand and inventory burden. Achieved cycle service level (CSL) measures the proportion of periods in which opening stock covers demand, and the lost-demand rate measures the share of demand left unmet. We report average opening inventory in the numerical experiment and opening months of stock and proxy opening inventory value in the empirical experiment. We also translate differences in stockout exposure into illustrative relative modern contraceptive prevalence rate (mCPR) loss, benchmarked against TCKF within each policy. The formulas and proxy-price sources are provided in **E-companion, Section 5**.
